title: DeepJoint: Robust Survival Modelling Under Clinical Presence Shift

en.text: A blood test ordered at 3 a.m., a lab panel repeated every hour, a measurement that simply never appears: to the clinician at the bedside, none of these is a random event. They reflect a judgment about who is sick and who needs watching. Yet most survival models trained on electronic health records treat the timing and the absence of measurements as noise, to be imputed away or ignored, and learn only from the recorded values.

The pattern of when and which tests get ordered, what the authors call clinical presence, is itself informative, and it is not stable. It differs between hospitals, drifts over the years, and changes even between a weekday and a weekend admission. A model that quietly learns one hospital's ordering habits can degrade when it is deployed somewhere those habits differ, which is exactly the situation any model faces the moment it leaves the dataset it was trained on.

DeepJoint (NeurIPS 2022), from the MRC Biostatistics Unit at the University of Cambridge and the Health e-Research Centre at the University of Manchester, asks what happens if we model the observation process explicitly instead of ignoring it. It is a single multi-task recurrent network that predicts three dimensions of clinical presence jointly with the survival outcome. The paper shows this both sharpens short-term predictions and, more importantly, makes them markedly more robust when clinical practice shifts.

en.caption: Figure 1. The Deep Joint Model. An LSTM turns a patient's irregular sequence of lab tests into an embedding h, which then feeds four heads: L models the longitudinal evolution of the values, I the inter-observation timing, M the missingness pattern, and S the survival outcome. Three of the four heads describe how the data are observed, not what they measure.

en.text: Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13481
Code: https://github.com/Jeanselme/MultitaskTransportability
Clinical presence: the observation process as signal

Machine learning has studied distribution shift for years, mostly as covariate shift (the inputs change) or label shift (the outcome balance changes). Clinical presence is a third, less-examined kind of shift: the process that generates the observations changes. The same underlying patient can look very different in the data depending on how closely they were monitored, and hospitals monitor differently.

The usual response is to make the sampling process disappear. Impute the missing values, resample onto a regular grid, and hand the model a clean matrix. DeepJoint takes the opposite view: the missingness, the timing, and the trajectory of the measurements carry information about the patient's state, so the model should learn them rather than erase them. The bet is that a representation that understands the observation process will both predict better and travel better.
One embedding, four heads

At the core is a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network that reads a patient's irregular sequence of laboratory tests after ICU admission and compresses it into an embedding h. That single embedding then drives four heads, each a small network with its own likelihood. The longitudinal head L predicts the next test values under a Gaussian likelihood; the missingness head M predicts which tests appear next under a Bernoulli likelihood; the inter-observation head I models the timing between measurements through a cumulative intensity; and the survival head S is a DeepSurv Cox model predicting the outcome.

All four heads are trained together. The survival loss and the three clinical-presence losses are combined into one objective, balanced by a hyperparameter alpha and a dynamic weighting-average scheme that keeps any single task from dominating: roughly, the loss is (1 - alpha) times the survival term plus alpha times a weighted sum of the longitudinal, timing, and missingness terms. Because the heads share h, forcing the embedding to explain how the data were observed regularizes it, which is what later pays off under shift.

The paper studies three variants of this idea. DeepJoint uses only the shared embedding for survival. DeepJointFeature adds explicit clinical-presence features on top of the embedding. DeepJointFineTune first trains the joint model, then fine-tunes the survival head end-to-end for maximum discrimination. As the results show, these three sit at different points on a trade-off between raw accuracy and robustness.
The data: 30,834 ICU patients from MIMIC-III

Experiments use MIMIC-III, the intensive-care database of anonymized labs, vitals, and diagnoses from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center covering 2001 to 2012. Of its 38,597 patients, the study keeps the 30,834 who survived at least the first 24 hours after admission, and predicts in-hospital survival from the embedding taken at the last observation within that first day. Models are compared on a 90% / 10% patient-level split using the time-dependent concordance index (C-index, higher is better) and the Brier score, at horizons of 1, 7, and 14 days.
Modelling the observation process pays off, on short horizons

On a random split of the population, the payoff is clearest at the one-day horizon. Read the figure below by row: each model's C-index at 1, 7, and 14 days, with 95% confidence intervals; the proposed methods are in bold. The telling comparison is at 1 day. DeepJoint, which sees only the laboratory values, reaches 0.862, ahead of the LSTM that ignores clinical presence (Ignore, 0.853) and of GRU-D (0.855), a strong baseline that explicitly consumes missingness as an input. Modelling the observation process, even without feeding it in, produces a more predictive embedding.

en.caption: Figure 2. Time-dependent C-index on a random split, at 1, 7, and 14 days (95% confidence intervals; higher is better). The proposed methods (bold) lead on the short horizon and converge with the baselines as the horizon lengthens, consistent with clinical presence signalling short-term instability.

en.text: Adding features and fine-tuning pushes further: DeepJointFeature reaches 0.873 and DeepJointFineTune 0.878 at one day, the best in the table. But the advantage is horizon-dependent. By 7 and 14 days the models bunch together, because clinical presence mostly signals short-term instability, how closely a patient is being watched right now, rather than their long-run trajectory. The table gives the exact numbers.

en.caption: Table 1. Time-dependent C-index (mean, higher is better) on a random population split. Proposed methods marked. The short-horizon edge is real but narrows by day 14.

en.text: The real test: surviving a shift in practice

Discrimination on a random split is the easy case, where train and test share the same observation process. The paper's central claim is about robustness, so it needs a controlled shift. It uses the weekend effect: patients admitted on weekends are monitored differently and are known to have different mortality from weekday admissions. That makes weekday-versus-weekend a natural, controllable change in the observation process.

Because the two groups also differ in outcome, their scores cannot be compared head to head. The paper instead borrows the robustness literature's transfer setup, shown below: train a model on one group and test it on the other, and separately train an oracle on the target group itself. Comparing the transferred model against its oracle isolates how much performance is lost purely to the shift in clinical presence.

en.caption: Figure 3. The robustness protocol. Model 1 trains on weekend admissions and is tested on weekday admissions; model 2 trains and tests within weekday admissions, serving as the oracle for that target group. The gap between them measures sensitivity to the shift, not to the outcome difference.

en.text: The result is read against the diagonal. In the figure below, each model's transferred performance (y-axis) is plotted against its oracle performance (x-axis) at all three horizons; a point on the dotted diagonal means the shift cost nothing. Points that fall below the line have lost accuracy to the change in observation process, and the further below, the less robust the model.

en.caption: Figure 4. Robustness under the weekday-to-weekend shift: transferred C-index (y-axis) versus oracle C-index (x-axis) across horizons; closer to the diagonal is more robust. DeepJointFeature (orange) sits nearest the diagonal while keeping strong discrimination; DeepJointFineTune (blue), the most accurate model on the random split, drops further below it.

en.text: Here the ranking flips. DeepJointFineTune, the sharpest model on the random split, sits further below the diagonal: fine-tuning hard for discrimination made it lean on the training group's specific ordering habits, so it overfits the observation process. DeepJointFeature stays closest to the diagonal while still discriminating well, making it the best all-round choice under shift. The accuracy champion and the robustness champion are not the same model, and the paper argues that for deployment the robust one is what matters.
Clinical presence is signal, not noise

The through-line is simple: how clinical data are observed, not just their recorded values, is information, and a model that learns the observation process alongside the outcome is both more accurate on short horizons and more transportable when practice changes. That reframes missingness and irregular timing from a preprocessing nuisance into something worth modelling directly.

The boundaries are worth stating plainly. The predictive edge is concentrated at short horizons and fades by two weeks; the study is a single database (MIMIC-III) and a single outcome (in-hospital survival); and the sharpest variant is also the one most prone to overfitting the observation process, so robustness has to be chosen for, not assumed. Still, the core message travels well beyond this dataset: when a model will be deployed somewhere its training habits do not hold, treating the observation process as signal is what lets its predictions survive the move.

zh.text: 凌晨三点开的一次血检、每小时重复的一组化验、始终没有出现的某项指标：在临床医生眼里，这些都不是随机事件，而是对「谁病得重、谁需要盯着」的判断。然而，大多数在电子病历上训练的生存模型，却把检测的时间和缺失当成噪声，要么插值补齐、要么直接忽略，只从记录下来的数值里学习。
什么时候、开哪些检查，这种模式本身就带着信息，作者称之为「临床在场（clinical presence，指临床数据被观测、采集的整个过程）」。更关键的是，它并不稳定：不同医院不一样，随年份漂移，甚至工作日入院和周末入院都不同。一个悄悄学到了某家医院开单习惯的模型，一旦部署到习惯不同的地方就可能失灵，而这恰恰是任何模型离开训练数据后都会遇到的处境。
DeepJoint（NeurIPS 2022）来自剑桥大学 MRC 生物统计中心与曼彻斯特大学 Health e-Research Centre，它问的问题是：如果不再忽略观测过程，而是把它明确地建模，会怎样？它是一个多任务循环网络，把临床在场的三个维度与生存结局一起预测。论文显示，这样做既让短期预测更准，更重要的是，当临床实践发生变化时，预测明显更稳。

zh.caption: 图1 DeepJoint 深度联合模型。一个 LSTM 把病人不规则的化验序列压成嵌入 h，再由 h 驱动四个「头」：L 负责数值的纵向演变，I 负责观测的间隔时间，M 负责缺失模式，S 负责生存结局。四个头里有三个描述的是数据「怎么被观测到」，而非「测到了什么」。

zh.text: 论文地址：https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13481
代码地址：https://github.com/Jeanselme/MultitaskTransportability
临床在场：把观测过程当成信号
机器学习研究分布漂移已有多年，大多集中在协变量漂移（covariate shift，输入变了）或标签漂移（label shift，结局比例变了）。临床在场是第三种、被讨论得少得多的漂移：产生观测的过程本身变了。同一个病人，因为被监护的密切程度不同，在数据里可以呈现出很不一样的样子，而各家医院的监护方式并不相同。
常见做法是想办法让采样过程「消失」：把缺失值补上、重采样到规则的时间网格，最后交给模型一个干净的矩阵。DeepJoint 的立场恰好相反：缺失、时间间隔、以及测量值的走势，都携带着病人状态的信息，模型应该去学习它们，而不是抹掉它们。这背后的赌注是，一个理解了观测过程的表示，既会预测得更好，也会迁移得更稳。
一个嵌入，四个头
模型的核心是一个 LSTM（长短期记忆网络）。它读入病人入住 ICU 后不规则的化验序列，压缩成一个嵌入 h。这个嵌入再驱动四个头，每个头都是一个小网络、带自己的似然：纵向头 L 用高斯似然预测下一次的检测数值；缺失头 M 用伯努利似然预测下一步会出现哪些检测；间隔头 I 用累积强度对测量之间的时间建模；生存头 S 则是一个 DeepSurv 的 Cox 模型，负责预测结局。

四个头一起训练。生存损失与三个临床在场损失被合成一个目标，由超参数 alpha 和一套动态加权平均（dynamic weighting-average）机制来平衡，避免任何单一任务主导：粗略地说，总损失是 (1 - alpha) 乘以生存项，加上 alpha 乘以纵向、间隔、缺失三项的加权和。由于四个头共享 h，强迫这个嵌入去解释「数据是怎么被观测的」，等于对它做了一层正则化，而这正是它在漂移下占便宜的原因。
论文给出三个变体。DeepJoint 只用共享嵌入做生存预测；DeepJointFeature 在嵌入之上再加入显式的临床在场特征；DeepJointFineTune 则先训练联合模型，再把生存头端到端微调，追求最强的区分度。后面的结果会看到，这三者落在「准确度」与「稳健性」权衡上的不同位置。
数据：MIMIC-III 的 30,834 名 ICU 病人

实验使用 MIMIC-III，这是一个重症监护数据库，收录了 Beth Israel Deaconess 医学中心 2001 到 2012 年间匿名的化验、生命体征与诊断。数据库共 38,597 名病人，研究保留了入院后至少存活 24 小时的 30,834 人，并用第一天窗口内最后一次观测时的嵌入来预测院内生存。模型在病人层面按 90% / 10% 划分，用时间依赖 C-index（一致性指数，越高越好）和 Brier 分数评估，预测时程为 1、7、14 天。
建模观测过程确有回报，但集中在短时程

在总体的随机划分上，回报在 1 天时程最明显。下图请按行读：每个模型在 1、7、14 天的 C-index，带 95% 置信区间，加粗的是本文方法。最能说明问题的是 1 天这一列。只看化验数值的 DeepJoint 达到 0.862，高于忽略临床在场的 LSTM（Ignore，0.853），也高于 GRU-D（0.855）这个把缺失当输入喂进去的强基线。也就是说，仅仅去建模观测过程，即便不把它作为输入，也能得到一个更有预测力的嵌入。

zh.caption: 图2 随机划分下的时间依赖 C-index，分别在 1、7、14 天（95% 置信区间，越高越好）。本文方法（加粗）在短时程领先，随着时程拉长逐渐与基线趋同，这与「临床在场主要反映短期不稳定」相吻合。

zh.text: 加特征、再微调能把成绩继续往上推：DeepJointFeature 在 1 天达到 0.873，DeepJointFineTune 达到 0.878，是全表最高。但优势依赖于时程。到 7 天、14 天，各模型基本挤到一起，因为临床在场更多反映的是短期不稳定，也就是「病人此刻被盯得有多紧」，而非长期走向。具体数字见下表。

zh.caption: 表1 随机划分下的时间依赖 C-index（均值，越高越好）。标注了本文方法。短时程的优势真实存在，但到第 14 天已明显收窄。

zh.text: 真正的考验：实践变了，模型还撑得住吗
随机划分上的区分度是简单情形，因为训练集和测试集共享同一套观测过程。论文真正想证明的是稳健性，因此需要一个可控的漂移。它用的是「周末效应」：周末入院的病人被监护的方式不同，其死亡率也已知与工作日入院不同。这就让「工作日 vs 周末」成为观测过程上一个天然、可控的变化。
由于两组病人的结局本身就有差异，它们的分数不能直接对比。论文转而借用稳健性文献里的迁移设置，如下图：在一组上训练、到另一组上测试，再单独在目标组自身上训练一个「oracle（理想上限）」模型。把迁移模型和它的 oracle 相比，就能单独分离出：有多少性能纯粹是被临床在场的漂移「吃掉」的。

zh.caption: 图3 稳健性评估协议。模型 1 在周末入院上训练、到工作日入院上测试；模型 2 在工作日入院内部训练并测试，作为该目标组的 oracle。两者的差距衡量的是对漂移的敏感度，而不是结局差异本身。

zh.text: 结果要对着对角线来读。下图中，每个模型的迁移表现（纵轴）对它的 oracle 表现（横轴）作图，覆盖三个时程；落在虚线对角线上，意味着漂移没有造成任何损失。落在线下方的点，就是把精度输给了观测过程的变化，越靠下，模型越不稳健。

zh.caption: 图4 工作日到周末漂移下的稳健性：迁移 C-index（纵轴）对 oracle C-index（横轴），覆盖各时程，越靠近对角线越稳健。DeepJointFeature（橙色）最贴近对角线，同时保持强区分度；而在随机划分上最准的 DeepJointFineTune（蓝色）掉得更靠下。

zh.text: 在这里，排名翻转了。在随机划分上最锋利的 DeepJointFineTune，此刻却更靠对角线下方：为了区分度而狠狠微调，让它依赖上了训练组特有的开单习惯，于是对观测过程发生了过拟合。DeepJointFeature 则最贴近对角线，同时仍有不错的区分度，成为漂移下综合最优的选择。准确度冠军和稳健性冠军并不是同一个模型，而论文认为：对于真正的部署，重要的是那个稳的。
临床在场是信号，不是噪声
贯穿全文的线索很朴素：临床数据「是怎么被观测到的」，而不只是记录下来的数值，本身就是信息；一个把观测过程和结局一起学习的模型，既在短时程上更准，也在实践变化时更能迁移。它把缺失和不规则时间，从预处理的麻烦重新定义为值得直接建模的信号。
边界也值得如实说清：预测优势集中在短时程，到两周时已消退；研究只基于单一数据库（MIMIC-III）和单一结局（院内生存）；而最锋利的那个变体，也正是最容易对观测过程过拟合的，稳健性得主动去选。但核心信息远不止这份数据：当模型要被部署到训练习惯并不成立的地方，把观测过程当成信号，正是让预测在迁移后依然站得住的关键。

DeepJoint takes the opposite view: the missingness, the timing, and the trajectory of the measurements carry information about the patient's state, so the model should learn them rather than erase them. zh.caption: 图1 DeepJoint 深度联合模型。一个 LSTM 把病人不规则的化验序列压成嵌入 h，再由 h 驱动四个「头」：L 负责数值的纵向演变，I 负责观测的间隔时间，M 负责缺失模式，S 负责生存结局。四个头里有三个描述的是数据「怎么被观测到」，而非「测到了什么」。

zh.text: 临床在场：把观测过程当成信号
机器学习研究分布漂移已有多年，大多集中在协变量漂移（covariate shift，输入变了）或标签漂移（label shift，结局比例变了）。临床在场是第三种、被讨论得少得多的漂移：产生观测的过程本身变了。同一个病人，因为被监护的密切程度不同，在数据里可以呈现出很不一样的样子，而各家医院的监护方式并不相同。
常见做法是想办法让采样过程「消失」：把缺失值补上、重采样到规则的时间网格，最后交给模型一个干净的矩阵。DeepJoint 的立场恰好相反：缺失、时间间隔、以及测量值的走势，都携带着病人状态的信息，模型应该去学习它们，而不是抹掉它们。这背后的赌注是，一个理解了观测过程的表示，既会预测得更好，也会迁移得更稳。

Model 1 trains on weekend admissions and is tested on weekday admissions; model 2 trains and tests within weekday admissions, serving as the oracle for that target group. The gap between them measures sensitivity to the shift, not to the outcome difference.

en.text: The data: 30,834 ICU patients from MIMIC-III

Experiments use MIMIC-III, the intensive-care database of anonymized labs, vitals, and diagnoses from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center covering 2001 to 2012. Of its 38,597 patients, the study keeps the 30,834 who survived at least the first 24 hours after admission, and predicts in-hospital survival from the embedding taken at the last observation within that first day. Models are compared on a 90% / 10% patient-level split using the time-dependent concordance index (C-index, higher is better) and the Brier score, at horizons of 1, 7, and 14 days.

zh.caption: 图1 DeepJoint 深度联合模型。一个 LSTM 把病人不规则的化验序列压成嵌入 h，再由 h 驱动四个「头」：L 负责数值的纵向演变，I 负责观测的间隔时间，M 负责缺失模式，S 负责生存结局。四个头里有三个描述的是数据「怎么被观测到」，而非「测到了什么」。

zh.text: 一个嵌入，四个头
模型的核心是一个 LSTM（长短期记忆网络）。它读入病人入住 ICU 后不规则的化验序列，压缩成一个嵌入 h。这个嵌入再驱动四个头，每个头都是一个小网络、带自己的似然：纵向头 L 用高斯似然预测下一次的检测数值；缺失头 M 用伯努利似然预测下一步会出现哪些检测；间隔头 I 用累积强度对测量之间的时间建模；生存头 S 则是一个 DeepSurv 的 Cox 模型，负责预测结局。

四个头一起训练。生存损失与三个临床在场损失被合成一个目标，由超参数 alpha 和一套动态加权平均（dynamic weighting-average）机制来平衡，避免任何单一任务主导：粗略地说，总损失是 (1 - alpha) 乘以生存项，加上 alpha 乘以纵向、间隔、缺失三项的加权和。由于四个头共享 h，强迫这个嵌入去解释「数据是怎么被观测的」，等于对它做了一层正则化，而这正是它在漂移下占便宜的原因。

en.text: Modelling the observation process pays off, on short horizons

On a random split of the population, the payoff is clearest at the one-day horizon. Read the figure below by row: each model's C-index at 1, 7, and 14 days, with 95% confidence intervals; the proposed methods are in bold. The telling comparison is at 1 day. DeepJoint, which sees only the laboratory values, reaches 0.862, ahead of the LSTM that ignores clinical presence (Ignore, 0.853) and of GRU-D (0.855), a strong baseline that explicitly consumes missingness as an input. Modelling the observation process, even without feeding it in, produces a more predictive embedding.

en.caption: Figure 2. Time-dependent C-index on a random split, at 1, 7, and 14 days (95% confidence intervals; higher is better). The proposed methods (bold) lead on the short horizon and converge with the baselines as the horizon lengthens, consistent with clinical presence signalling short-term instability.

en.text: Adding features and fine-tuning pushes further: DeepJointFeature reaches 0.873 and DeepJointFineTune 0.878 at one day, the best in the table. But the advantage is horizon-dependent. By 7 and 14 days the models bunch together, because clinical presence mostly signals short-term instability, how closely a patient is being watched right now, rather than their long-run trajectory. The table gives the exact numbers.

en.caption: Table 1. Time-dependent C-index (mean, higher is better) on a random population split. Proposed methods marked. The short-horizon edge is real but narrows by day 14.

zh.text: 建模观测过程确有回报，但集中在短时程

zh.caption: 图2 随机划分下的时间依赖 C-index，分别在 1、7、14 天（95% 置信区间，越高越好）。本文方法（加粗）在短时程领先，随着时程拉长逐渐与基线趋同，这与「临床在场主要反映短期不稳定」相吻合。

zh.text: 加特征、再微调能把成绩继续往上推：DeepJointFeature 在 1 天达到 0.873，DeepJointFineTune 达到 0.878，是全表最高。但优势依赖于时程。到 7 天、14 天，各模型基本挤到一起，因为临床在场更多反映的是短期不稳定，也就是「病人此刻被盯得有多紧」，而非长期走向。具体数字见下表。

en.text: A blood test ordered at 3 a.m., a lab panel repeated every hour, a measurement that simply never appears: to the clinician at the bedside, none of these is a random event. They reflect a judgment about who is sick and who needs watching. Yet most survival models trained on electronic health records treat the timing and the absence of measurements as noise, to be imputed away or ignored, and learn only from the recorded values.

The pattern of when and which tests get ordered, what the authors call clinical presence, is itself informative, and it is not stable. It differs between hospitals, drifts over the years, and changes even between a weekday and a weekend admission. A model that quietly learns one hospital's ordering habits can degrade when it is deployed somewhere those habits differ, which is exactly the situation any model faces the moment it leaves the dataset it was trained on.

DeepJoint (NeurIPS 2022), from the MRC Biostatistics Unit at the University of Cambridge and the Health e-Research Centre at the University of Manchester, asks what happens if we model the observation process explicitly instead of ignoring it. It is a single multi-task recurrent network that predicts three dimensions of clinical presence jointly with the survival outcome. The paper shows this both sharpens short-term predictions and, more importantly, makes them markedly more robust when clinical practice shifts.

An LSTM turns a patient's irregular sequence of lab tests into an embedding h, which then feeds four heads: L models the longitudinal evolution of the values, I the inter-observation timing, M the missingness pattern, and S the survival outcome. Three of the four heads describe how the data are observed, not what they measure.

en.title: NeurIPS 2022 | When Missing Data Is a Signal: Making Clinical Survival Models Robust
en.subtitle: DeepJoint, from the University of Cambridge and the University of Manchester, models how clinical data are observed, not just their values, and stays accurate when hospital practice shifts.

zh.title: NeurIPS 2022 | 缺失也是信息：让临床生存模型在实践变化时依然可靠
zh.subtitle: 剑桥大学与曼彻斯特大学提出 DeepJoint，把「数据是怎么被观测到的」也一起建模，而不只看数值本身。

en.text: One embedding, four heads

At the core is a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network that reads a patient's irregular sequence of laboratory tests after ICU admission and compresses it into an embedding h. That single embedding then drives four heads, each a small network with its own likelihood. The longitudinal head L predicts the next test values under a Gaussian likelihood; the missingness head M predicts which tests appear next under a Bernoulli likelihood; the inter-observation head I models the timing between measurements through a cumulative intensity; and the survival head S is a DeepSurv Cox model predicting the outcome.

All four heads are trained together. The survival loss and the three clinical-presence losses are combined into one objective, balanced by a hyperparameter alpha and a dynamic weighting-average scheme that keeps any single task from dominating: roughly, the loss is (1 - alpha) times the survival term plus alpha times a weighted sum of the longitudinal, timing, and missingness terms. Because the heads share h, forcing the embedding to explain how the data were observed regularizes it, which is what later pays off under shift.

The paper studies three variants of this idea. DeepJoint uses only the shared embedding for survival. DeepJointFeature adds explicit clinical-presence features on top of the embedding. DeepJointFineTune first trains the joint model, then fine-tunes the survival head end-to-end for maximum discrimination. As the results show, these three sit at different points on a trade-off between raw accuracy and robustness.
The real test: surviving a shift in practice

Discrimination on a random split is the easy case, where train and test share the same observation process. The paper's central claim is about robustness, so it needs a controlled shift. It uses the weekend effect: patients admitted on weekends are monitored differently and are known to have different mortality from weekday admissions. That makes weekday-versus-weekend a natural, controllable change in the observation process.

Because the two groups also differ in outcome, their scores cannot be compared head to head. The paper instead borrows the robustness literature's transfer setup, shown below: train a model on one group and test it on the other, and separately train an oracle on the target group itself. Comparing the transferred model against its oracle isolates how much performance is lost purely to the shift in clinical presence.

en.caption: Figure 3. The robustness protocol. Model 1 trains on weekend admissions and is tested on weekday admissions; model 2 trains and tests within weekday admissions, serving as the oracle for that target group. The gap between them measures sensitivity to the shift, not to the outcome difference.

en.text: The result is read against the diagonal. In the figure below, each model's transferred performance (y-axis) is plotted against its oracle performance (x-axis) at all three horizons; a point on the dotted diagonal means the shift cost nothing. Points that fall below the line have lost accuracy to the change in observation process, and the further below, the less robust the model.

en.caption: Figure 4. Robustness under the weekday-to-weekend shift: transferred C-index (y-axis) versus oracle C-index (x-axis) across horizons; closer to the diagonal is more robust. DeepJointFeature (orange) sits nearest the diagonal while keeping strong discrimination; DeepJointFineTune (blue), the most accurate model on the random split, drops further below it.

en.text: Here the ranking flips. DeepJointFineTune, the sharpest model on the random split, sits further below the diagonal: fine-tuning hard for discrimination made it lean on the training group's specific ordering habits, so it overfits the observation process. DeepJointFeature stays closest to the diagonal while still discriminating well, making it the best all-round choice under shift. The accuracy champion and the robustness champion are not the same model, and the paper argues that for deployment the robust one is what matters.

zh.text: 一个嵌入，四个头
模型的核心是一个 LSTM（长短期记忆网络）。它读入病人入住 ICU 后不规则的化验序列，压缩成一个嵌入 h。这个嵌入再驱动四个头，每个头都是一个小网络、带自己的似然：纵向头 L 用高斯似然预测下一次的检测数值；缺失头 M 用伯努利似然预测下一步会出现哪些检测；间隔头 I 用累积强度对测量之间的时间建模；生存头 S 则是一个 DeepSurv 的 Cox 模型，负责预测结局。

四个头一起训练。生存损失与三个临床在场损失被合成一个目标，由超参数 alpha 和一套动态加权平均（dynamic weighting-average）机制来平衡，避免任何单一任务主导：粗略地说，总损失是 (1 - alpha) 乘以生存项，加上 alpha 乘以纵向、间隔、缺失三项的加权和。由于四个头共享 h，强迫这个嵌入去解释「数据是怎么被观测的」，等于对它做了一层正则化，而这正是它在漂移下占便宜的原因。
论文给出三个变体。DeepJoint 只用共享嵌入做生存预测；DeepJointFeature 在嵌入之上再加入显式的临床在场特征；DeepJointFineTune 则先训练联合模型，再把生存头端到端微调，追求最强的区分度。后面的结果会看到，这三者落在「准确度」与「稳健性」权衡上的不同位置。
真正的考验：实践变了，模型还撑得住吗
随机划分上的区分度是简单情形，因为训练集和测试集共享同一套观测过程。论文真正想证明的是稳健性，因此需要一个可控的漂移。它用的是「周末效应」：周末入院的病人被监护的方式不同，其死亡率也已知与工作日入院不同。这就让「工作日 vs 周末」成为观测过程上一个天然、可控的变化。
由于两组病人的结局本身就有差异，它们的分数不能直接对比。论文转而借用稳健性文献里的迁移设置，如下图：在一组上训练、到另一组上测试，再单独在目标组自身上训练一个「oracle（理想上限）」模型。把迁移模型和它的 oracle 相比，就能单独分离出：有多少性能纯粹是被临床在场的漂移「吃掉」的。

zh.caption: 图3 稳健性评估协议。模型 1 在周末入院上训练、到工作日入院上测试；模型 2 在工作日入院内部训练并测试，作为该目标组的 oracle。两者的差距衡量的是对漂移的敏感度，而不是结局差异本身。

zh.text: 结果要对着对角线来读。下图中，每个模型的迁移表现（纵轴）对它的 oracle 表现（横轴）作图，覆盖三个时程；落在虚线对角线上，意味着漂移没有造成任何损失。落在线下方的点，就是把精度输给了观测过程的变化，越靠下，模型越不稳健。

zh.caption: 图4 工作日到周末漂移下的稳健性：迁移 C-index（纵轴）对 oracle C-index（横轴），覆盖各时程，越靠近对角线越稳健。DeepJointFeature（橙色）最贴近对角线，同时保持强区分度；而在随机划分上最准的 DeepJointFineTune（蓝色）掉得更靠下。

zh.text: 在这里，排名翻转了。在随机划分上最锋利的 DeepJointFineTune，此刻却更靠对角线下方：为了区分度而狠狠微调，让它依赖上了训练组特有的开单习惯，于是对观测过程发生了过拟合。DeepJointFeature 则最贴近对角线，同时仍有不错的区分度，成为漂移下综合最优的选择。准确度冠军和稳健性冠军并不是同一个模型，而论文认为：对于真正的部署，重要的是那个稳的。

en.subtitle: DeepJoint, from the University of Cambridge and the University of Manchester, models how clinical data are observed, not just their values, and stays accurate when hospital practice shifts.

zh.title: NeurIPS 2022 | 缺失也是信息：让临床生存模型在实践变化时依然可靠
zh.subtitle: 剑桥大学与曼彻斯特大学提出 DeepJoint，把「数据是怎么被观测到的」也一起建模，而不只看数值本身。

en.caption: Figure 1. The Deep Joint Model. An LSTM turns a patient's irregular sequence of lab tests into an embedding h, which then feeds four heads: L models the longitudinal evolution of the values, I the inter-observation timing, M the missingness pattern, and S the survival outcome. Three of the four heads describe how the data are observed, not what they measure.

en.text: Clinical presence is signal, not noise

The through-line is simple: how clinical data are observed, not just their recorded values, is information, and a model that learns the observation process alongside the outcome is both more accurate on short horizons and more transportable when practice changes. That reframes missingness and irregular timing from a preprocessing nuisance into something worth modelling directly.

The boundaries are worth stating plainly. The predictive edge is concentrated at short horizons and fades by two weeks; the study is a single database (MIMIC-III) and a single outcome (in-hospital survival); and the sharpest variant is also the one most prone to overfitting the observation process, so robustness has to be chosen for, not assumed. Still, the core message travels well beyond this dataset: when a model will be deployed somewhere its training habits do not hold, treating the observation process as signal is what lets its predictions survive the move.

zh.caption: 图1 DeepJoint 深度联合模型。一个 LSTM 把病人不规则的化验序列压成嵌入 h，再由 h 驱动四个「头」：L 负责数值的纵向演变，I 负责观测的间隔时间，M 负责缺失模式，S 负责生存结局。四个头里有三个描述的是数据「怎么被观测到」，而非「测到了什么」。

zh.text: 临床在场是信号，不是噪声
贯穿全文的线索很朴素：临床数据「是怎么被观测到的」，而不只是记录下来的数值，本身就是信息；一个把观测过程和结局一起学习的模型，既在短时程上更准，也在实践变化时更能迁移。它把缺失和不规则时间，从预处理的麻烦重新定义为值得直接建模的信号。
边界也值得如实说清：预测优势集中在短时程，到两周时已消退；研究只基于单一数据库（MIMIC-III）和单一结局（院内生存）；而最锋利的那个变体，也正是最容易对观测过程过拟合的，稳健性得主动去选。但核心信息远不止这份数据：当模型要被部署到训练习惯并不成立的地方，把观测过程当成信号，正是让预测在迁移后依然站得住的关键。

zh.text: 建模观测过程确有回报，但集中在短时程

在总体的随机划分上，回报在 1 天时程最明显。下图请按行读：每个模型在 1、7、14 天的 C-index，带 95% 置信区间，加粗的是本文方法。最能说明问题的是 1 天这一列。只看化验数值的 DeepJoint 达到 0.862，高于忽略临床在场的 LSTM（Ignore，0.853），也高于 GRU-D（0.855）这个把缺失当输入喂进去的强基线。也就是说，仅仅去建模观测过程，即便不把它作为输入，也能得到一个更有预测力的嵌入。

zh.caption: 图2 随机划分下的时间依赖 C-index，分别在 1、7、14 天（95% 置信区间，越高越好）。本文方法（加粗）在短时程领先，随着时程拉长逐渐与基线趋同，这与「临床在场主要反映短期不稳定」相吻合。

zh.text: 加特征、再微调能把成绩继续往上推：DeepJointFeature 在 1 天达到 0.873，DeepJointFineTune 达到 0.878，是全表最高。但优势依赖于时程。到 7 天、14 天，各模型基本挤到一起，因为临床在场更多反映的是短期不稳定，也就是「病人此刻被盯得有多紧」，而非长期走向。具体数字见下表。

An LSTM turns a patient's irregular sequence of lab tests into an embedding h, which then feeds four heads: L models the longitudinal evolution of the values, I the inter-observation timing, M the missingness pattern, and S the survival outcome. en.text: Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13481
Code: https://github.com/Jeanselme/MultitaskTransportability
The real test: surviving a shift in practice

Discrimination on a random split is the easy case, where train and test share the same observation process. The paper's central claim is about robustness, so it needs a controlled shift. It uses the weekend effect: patients admitted on weekends are monitored differently and are known to have different mortality from weekday admissions. That makes weekday-versus-weekend a natural, controllable change in the observation process.

Because the two groups also differ in outcome, their scores cannot be compared head to head. The paper instead borrows the robustness literature's transfer setup, shown below: train a model on one group and test it on the other, and separately train an oracle on the target group itself. Comparing the transferred model against its oracle isolates how much performance is lost purely to the shift in clinical presence.

en.caption: Figure 3. The robustness protocol. Model 1 trains on weekend admissions and is tested on weekday admissions; model 2 trains and tests within weekday admissions, serving as the oracle for that target group. The gap between them measures sensitivity to the shift, not to the outcome difference.

en.text: The result is read against the diagonal. In the figure below, each model's transferred performance (y-axis) is plotted against its oracle performance (x-axis) at all three horizons; a point on the dotted diagonal means the shift cost nothing. Points that fall below the line have lost accuracy to the change in observation process, and the further below, the less robust the model.

en.caption: Figure 4. Robustness under the weekday-to-weekend shift: transferred C-index (y-axis) versus oracle C-index (x-axis) across horizons; closer to the diagonal is more robust. DeepJointFeature (orange) sits nearest the diagonal while keeping strong discrimination; DeepJointFineTune (blue), the most accurate model on the random split, drops further below it.

en.text: Here the ranking flips. DeepJointFineTune, the sharpest model on the random split, sits further below the diagonal: fine-tuning hard for discrimination made it lean on the training group's specific ordering habits, so it overfits the observation process. DeepJointFeature stays closest to the diagonal while still discriminating well, making it the best all-round choice under shift. The accuracy champion and the robustness champion are not the same model, and the paper argues that for deployment the robust one is what matters.

zh.caption: 图1 DeepJoint 深度联合模型。一个 LSTM 把病人不规则的化验序列压成嵌入 h，再由 h 驱动四个「头」：L 负责数值的纵向演变，I 负责观测的间隔时间，M 负责缺失模式，S 负责生存结局。四个头里有三个描述的是数据「怎么被观测到」，而非「测到了什么」。

zh.text: 临床在场是信号，不是噪声
贯穿全文的线索很朴素：临床数据「是怎么被观测到的」，而不只是记录下来的数值，本身就是信息；一个把观测过程和结局一起学习的模型，既在短时程上更准，也在实践变化时更能迁移。它把缺失和不规则时间，从预处理的麻烦重新定义为值得直接建模的信号。
边界也值得如实说清：预测优势集中在短时程，到两周时已消退；研究只基于单一数据库（MIMIC-III）和单一结局（院内生存）；而最锋利的那个变体，也正是最容易对观测过程过拟合的，稳健性得主动去选。但核心信息远不止这份数据：当模型要被部署到训练习惯并不成立的地方，把观测过程当成信号，正是让预测在迁移后依然站得住的关键。
